title: Episode 36: The Great Seattle Fire and the Underground City
description:
On June 6, 1889, a cabinetmaker's apprentice accidentally overturned a pot of boiling glue on a wood shavings floor, sparking the Great Seattle Fire. Burning thirty-two blocks to the ground, the catastrophe spurred citizens to rebuild with stone and elevate the street level by up to thirty feet, encasing the original first-floor storefronts and sidewalks completely underground.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In eighteen eighty-nine, Seattle was an explosive, muddy timber boomtown on the shores of Puget Sound. Built almost entirely out of Douglas fir lumber atop tidal mudflats, the city was so low that twice a day at high tide, saltwater backed up through wooden sewer pipes, bursting through tavern toilets. On a scorching June afternoon, an apprentice cabinetmaker accidentally tipped over a cast-iron pot of boiling animal glue onto a dry wood-shavings floor. Within hours, thirty-two city blocks were transformed into a raging inferno that consumed the entire business district. But in the ashes of catastrophe, Seattle's citizens devised an audacious engineering solution: they elevated the city streets by up to thirty feet, burying the burned ruins and creating an entire subterranean ghost city beneath modern sidewalks. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE MUDDY TIMBER METROPOLIS
In the spring of eighteen eighty-nine, Seattle, Washington was a roaring, chaotic frontier port perched on the shores of Elliott Bay. Fueled by the booming lumber industry and transcontinental railroad connections, the population had exploded to more than thirty thousand people. Yet the physical city was an engineering disaster waiting to happen. Seattle was constructed almost entirely out of highly flammable Douglas fir lumber—wooden buildings, wooden sidewalks, wooden bridges, and even hollowed-out wooden log pipes for municipal water and sewers. Even worse was the topography: the commercial center along Pioneer Square was situated on low-lying tidal mudflats at the base of steep hills. Whenever Puget Sound's tide came in, the seawater backed up into the crude sewage lines, causing plumbing to burst and filling basements with noxious sludge. Streets were rivers of deep, sticky clay mud that swallowed horses and wagons. The city possessed a volunteer fire department, but its equipment was primitive and water pressure was dangerously erratic, supplied by a patchwork network of private spring companies that ran wooden mains through the sawdust streets. Puget Sound was packed with steamships and timber schooners shipping lumber to rebuild San Francisco and supply railroads across the continent. Thousands of Scandinavian and Canadian lumberjacks crowded into wooden boarding houses along the muddy tidal flats of Elliott Bay. Wharves groaned under the weight of colossal cedar logs, while sawmills operated round the clock, filling the sea air with the fragrant scent of freshly cut timber and burning sawdust.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SPILLED GLUE POT
The catastrophic spark was struck on the sweltering afternoon of Thursday, June sixth, eighteen eighty-nine. In the basement of Victor Clairmont's cabinetmaking shop at the corner of First Avenue and Madison Street, a young Swedish apprentice named John Back was heating a cast-iron pot of glue over an open gasoline stove. Around two-thirty in the afternoon, the glue overheated and boiled over, spilling onto a floor covered with bone-dry cedar shavings and turpentine. A sheet of flame instantly engulfed the workbench. In a panic, Back threw a bucket of water onto the fire, but because the blaze was fueled by burning grease and turpentine, the water only spread the flaming liquid across the entire workshop floor. Back and fellow workers scrambled out into the street, shouting for help. By the time volunteer firemen arrived with their hand-drawn hose cart, the wooden walls of the carpentry shop were fully involved, and fierce twenty-mile-per-hour gusts of wind from Elliott Bay were blowing embers onto neighboring wooden roofs. The glue pot was bubbling over an open gas flame when twenty-four-year-old carpenter John Back attempted to cool the boiling mixture with kerosene, instantly triggering an explosive fireball that set the wood shavings on the workshop floor roaring into flame. Within minutes of ignition, flames leaped to adjacent paint barrels and turpentine cans stored near the workshop doors, sending rolling clouds of black petroleum smoke curling into the summer sky.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THIRTY-TWO BLOCKS IN FIRE AND ROARING DYNAMITE
Within an hour, the fire had grown beyond human control. Embers landed on the dry shake roofs of commercial saloons, hotels, hardware stores, and wholesale liquor warehouses. When firemen attempted to connect their canvas hoses to municipal hydrants, they discovered to their horror that water pressure had plummeted to zero; the private water company was run by rival firms that had failed to connect their mains, and thousands of residents were simultaneously drawing water from taps to protect their homes. Seattle Mayor Robert Moran, a former shipbuilder, took personal command of the crisis. Realizing that water was useless, Moran ordered volunteer crews to use dynamite to blow up buildings in the path of the flames to create a firebreak. But the dynamite was mishandled, only shattering buildings into kindling that caught fire faster. By dusk, thirty-two entire square blocks—spanning over one hundred and twenty acres of the city's commercial and industrial heart—were an unbroken sea of flames. The heat was so intense that iron safes melted into puddles, plate-glass windows liquefied, and entire wooden wharves along the waterfront collapsed into the bay with hissing roars. The city Volunteer Fire Department arrived with horse-drawn steam pumpers, but the water pressure in the wooden hollowed-log mains failed completely. Fire Chief Gardner Kellogg made the agonizing decision to use gunpowder to blast entire city blocks into rubble, hoping to create a firebreak. Citizens formed desperate bucket brigades along Commercial Street, passing tin pails from Elliott Bay until the radiant heat blistered their hands and forced them to abandon the hoses to the roaring conflagration.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: MAYOR MORAN'S DECREE: BRICK, STONE, AND ELEVATED STREETS
Miraculously, despite the catastrophic destruction, not a single human life was lost in the Great Seattle Fire, though thousands of horses, rats, and pets perished. By the morning of June seventh, Seattle's business district was a smoldering, leveled wasteland of white ash and twisted iron. But rather than despair, the citizens displayed an electrifying frontier resilience. Mayor Moran called a mass town meeting in the armory that very morning. The city council enacted two immediate, revolutionary decrees: first, all future buildings in the fire district must be constructed strictly out of brick, stone, or iron; and second, the city would permanently solve its tidal mud and sewage nightmares by radically regrading the city, raising the overall street level anywhere from twelve to thirty feet above the original mudflats. Mayor Robert Moran called an emergency meeting of business leaders while the ashes were still smoking. He declared that wooden architecture was forbidden forever, mandating that the new Seattle rise in solid brick, stone, and fireproof iron. Surveyors and stone masons arrived from San Francisco and Chicago on chartered steamers, bringing drafting tables and transit levels to layout wider avenues engineered with underground utility conduits.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SUNKEN SIDEWALKS AND THE LADDERS OF PIONEER SQUARE
The decision to raise the streets created one of the most surreal construction dilemmas in urban history. Because business owners could not wait years for the city to finish regrading before reopening, they immediately began building their new brick buildings on the original, low-lying ground level. Meanwhile, city engineering crews constructed massive concrete and stone retaining walls along the curbs of the streets and filled the roadbeds between the walls with hundreds of thousands of tons of earth washed down from surrounding hills with hydraulic cannons. This left the paved streets perched twenty feet in the air, while the sidewalks and building entrances remained down in deep, sunken canyons! For several years, Seattle pedestrians had to use wooden ladders to climb down from the street level to enter shops on the original ground floor, and climb back up to cross the street. Eventually, the city bridged the gap by paving over the sunken sidewalks with concrete sidewalks supported by steel beams, embedding thousands of small purple glass prism skylights to illuminate the subterranean pedestrian passages below. What had been the original ground-floor storefronts were now dark basements, completely enclosed underground. Pedestrians in Pioneer Square had to navigate streets thirty feet higher than the storefront entrances, climbing wooden ladders to enter ground-floor retail shops while horse-drawn carriages rattled overhead along the new elevated avenues.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE SEALED LABYRINTH AND THE BUBONIC PLAGUE
For decades, the Seattle Underground was a shadowy, forbidden labyrinth beneath Pioneer Square. During the Klondike Gold Rush and Prohibition, the dark subterranean passages housed speakeasies, opium dens, gambling joints, and flophouses, accessible only through secret trapdoors. But in nineteen oh-seven, fear of the bubonic plague prompted the city health department to officially condemn and seal off the entire underground network with heavy iron doors, and the buried city was largely forgotten. Water dripped down brick arches, dust settled over antique barber chairs, and the subterranean avenues slept in pitch darkness while modern automobiles rumbled above. Below the street level, a hidden city flourished in the shadowed tunnels, where illicit gambling halls, speakeasies, and pawnshops operated away from the gaze of city marshals, until a health panic sealed the subterranean entrances with iron doors.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: BILL SPEIDEL AND THE RESURRECTED CITY BENEATH THE STREETS
In the nineteen sixties, a passionate local historian and journalist named Bill Speidel rediscovered the forgotten underground passages. Fighting against city planners who wanted to demolish historic Pioneer Square for modern parking garages, Speidel cleared away tons of debris and launched the world-famous Seattle Underground Tour. Today, visitors from around the globe can walk through the dark, brick-lined tunnels beneath modern Pioneer Square, gazing through dusty glass windows into nineteenth-century saloons, bank vaults, and storefronts that were buried alive in eighteen eighty-nine. The Great Seattle Fire and the city beneath the streets stand as an unforgettable testament to a city that refused to be defeated by flames, choosing instead to elevate itself above its troubles. Speidel underground tours breathed new life into the historic district, transforming damp, forgotten alleys into one of the Northwest most beloved tourist destinations, celebrated as a living testament to pioneer resilience.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Great Seattle Fire and the Underground City reveal how disaster can become the catalyst for extraordinary reinvention and architectural imagination. It proves that what lies beneath our feet is often just as fascinating as what towers above. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday as we witness the dramatic flutter and collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge. Until then, stay curious.
